lessons.title: Epidemiological foundations
lessons.objective: Define the population, outcome, denominator and time period before choosing an analysis.
lessons.summary: Define the population, selection process, outcome and time horizon first. Prevalence counts existing cases in a population at a specified time or period. Incidence concerns new cases: cumulative risk concerns initially disease-free people over a fixed period, whereas an incidence rate uses their time at risk. Changing diagnosis counts can reflect population size, testing or case definitions, not just disease occurrence. Study design and ascertainment determine what comparisons mean.
lessons.challenge: A clinic sees twice as many new diagnoses this year. Which population, testing and time-period information would you need before concluding that disease risk has doubled?
lessons.steps: This fictional one-year cohort starts with 300 disease-free exposed and 300 disease-free unexposed people, with complete follow-up and comparable case ascertainment. There are 30 and 15 first cases respectively. The risk form takes four cell counts, not group totals: columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent. Enter top row 30, 15 and bottom row 270, 285. Then one-year risks are 10% and 5%, RR = 2 and exposed-minus-unexposed risk difference = 5 percentage points. These are observational associations; they do not by themselves establish an exposure effect.
lessons.r:
# Fictional cohort: initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up,
# comparable case ascertainment; events are first cases in distinct people.
events <- c(30,15); at_risk <- c(300,300)
print(data.frame(Group=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),Events=events,At_risk=at_risk,Risk=events/at_risk))
print(c(risk_ratio=(30/300)/(15/300),risk_difference=30/300-15/300))
barplot(events/at_risk,names.arg=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylim=c(0,0.15),ylab="One-year risk",main="Observed association, not a causal estimate")
# If follow-up durations differ, examine person-time and censoring; do not label these risks incidence rates.

lessons.title: From association to causal questions
lessons.objective: Recognise confounding and define the assumptions behind a causal comparison.
lessons.summary: A causal question compares well-defined alternatives in the same target population. Baseline age can influence exposure and outcome, making the exposed groups incomparable. Adjustment needs a justified causal structure and assumptions, not just a change in an estimate. Conditioning on a mediator can remove part of a total effect and does not automatically identify a direct effect; conditioning on a common consequence can induce selection bias.
lessons.challenge: Age can affect both treatment choice and outcome. Why might adjusting for age help, while adjusting for a consequence of treatment change the effect we are trying to estimate?
lessons.steps: Assume initially disease-free people, complete one-year follow-up and age measured before exposure. Constructed counts are 44/200 exposed versus 26/200 unexposed. For the crude risk grid, columns are exposed/unexposed and rows are outcome present/absent: enter top row 44, 26 and bottom row 156, 174. Younger risks are 4/40 and 16/160; older risks are 40/160 and 10/40. Crude RR is about 1.69, but each within-age RR is 1. Standardising both groups to a 50% younger, 50% older population gives risk 17.5% in each. This illustrates age imbalance; neither equality after adjustment nor a crude association proves a causal conclusion.
lessons.r:
# Constructed baseline-age example: initially disease-free people,
# first cases over one year with complete follow-up. Age precedes exposure.
data <- data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),Exposed_events=c(4,40),Exposed_total=c(40,160),Unexposed_events=c(16,10),Unexposed_total=c(160,40))
data$Exposed_risk <- data$Exposed_events/data$Exposed_total
data$Unexposed_risk <- data$Unexposed_events/data$Unexposed_total
print(data)
print(c(crude_RR=(44/200)/(26/200)))
print(data.frame(Age=data$Age,Within_age_RR=data$Exposed_risk/data$Unexposed_risk))
# Apply the SAME target-population weights to both groups.
weights <- c(0.5,0.5)
standardised <- c(Exposed=sum(weights*data$Exposed_risk),Unexposed=sum(weights*data$Unexposed_risk))
print(standardised)
print(c(standardised_RR=unname(standardised[1]/standardised[2])))
barplot(rbind(data$Exposed_risk,data$Unexposed_risk),beside=TRUE,names.arg=data$Age,legend.text=c("Exposed","Unexposed"),ylab="Observed risk",main="Same within-age risks; different age mix")
# Within-stratum agreement is not proof that every source of bias has been removed.

keyConcepts.explanation: Ask what would happen under each well-defined exposure strategy in the same target population. Specify follow-up and the effect scale before analysing.

Exchangeability means the compared groups are comparable for their potential outcomes after justified adjustment. Positivity requires both alternatives to be possible in relevant strata; consistency links observed outcomes to the specified exposure.
Use temporal ordering and subject knowledge to choose covariates. A confounder precedes exposure; a mediator carries part of its effect; selecting on a common consequence can induce association.

misconceptions.claim: Equal age-adjusted risks prove there is no causal effect.

lessons.title: Comparing paired measurements
lessons.objective: Recognise pairing, analyse differences and interpret a confidence interval.
lessons.summary: Pairing means repeated measurements on the same people or explicitly matched units. A paired t test analyses within-pair differences, with independence between pairs. For exact small-sample inference the differences are normally distributed; inspect their distribution and unusual values. Two sets of patients attending the same clinic at different times are not automatically paired, and different patients may still be clustered.
lessons.challenge: The example has a before and an after measurement on each of the same eight people. Why is a paired analysis appropriate, and what design questions would you ask if the two periods instead contained different, unmatched people?
lessons.steps: Use Try in StatsDirect to open the paired t test with Before and After. The worksheet contains eight fictional, independently sampled participants. The comparison is Before minus After, so a positive difference means a fall. Use a 95% confidence level to compare with the R example. Inspect the differences and interpret the estimated mean difference and interval before the P value; an uncontrolled before–after change alone does not establish causation.
lessons.r:
# Fictional paired measurements: same eight people, same row order.
before <- c(142,136,151,145,139,148,132,155)
after <- c(135,134,143,141,136,140,130,147)
data <- data.frame(Before=before, After=after)
print(data)
# StatsDirect uses first minus second for this selection.
# Assume independent people; small-sample t inference models normal differences.
change <- before - after
print(t.test(before, after, paired=TRUE, conf.level=0.95))
plot(before, after, pch=19, xlab="Before", ylab="After", main="Fictional paired measurements")
abline(0,1,lty=2)
# The diagonal shows equal before/after values; this is not an agreement analysis.
# Try: inspect change, change one after value, rerun, and explain the interval.
# A change without a suitable control comparison does not establish causation.
previousChallenges: If the average measurement falls after an intervention, what else would you need before claiming the intervention caused the change?

The same eight people have a measurement taken before and after an intervention, with each person's two values on the same row. Why are these paired observations? How would the analysis change if different people were measured in the two periods?

keyConcepts.explanation: Each row must contain measurements from the same person or explicitly matched units. Reordering only one column destroys the design.

A high correlation does not establish agreement between methods. An uncontrolled before–after change also permits time trends, regression to the mean and other explanations.

misconceptions.claim: Before and after labels automatically imply pairing.
misconceptions.correction: Different unmatched people need a design-appropriate independent or clustered analysis.

misconceptions.claim: A normality test with P > 0.05 proves the differences are normal.
misconceptions.correction: Small samples provide weak evidence about shape; inspect the differences and unusual observations.

workedExample.interpretation: The mean reduction is 5.25 units. Interpret the interval for the population mean difference, not as the spread of individual changes or proof of an intervention effect.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Would a small mean difference between two measurement methods establish interchangeability?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: No. Inspect limits of agreement and whether their width is acceptable for the intended use.

lessons.title: Variation, precision and uncertainty
lessons.objective: Separate standard deviation from standard error and confidence intervals.
lessons.summary: Standard deviation describes variation between observations. Standard error describes sampling variation of an estimator. For independent observations from the same population, the mean has SE = population SD / sqrt(n), estimated using the sample SD. A nominal 95% confidence procedure targets 95% repeated-sampling coverage under its assumptions. These 12 waits are skewed: a small-sample t interval is an illustration to scrutinise, not an assurance of reliable coverage.
lessons.challenge: For independent observations from the same population with a fixed, finite variance, why does quadrupling sample size halve the theoretical standard error of the mean? Why might the sample SD and estimated SE still vary between samples?
lessons.steps: Open the descriptive summary for the fictional waiting times. Compare mean, median, SD and the 95% confidence interval. Inspect the long wait and the distribution before interpreting the small-sample t interval. Do not delete an observation merely because it is large. The appropriate summary depends on whether the question concerns an average, a typical wait or the long-wait tail. For these 12 values, StatsDirect and R t.test() both use a Student t interval for the mean with 11 degrees of freedom: approximately 13.8 to 24.8 minutes. Agreement between programs checks the calculation, not whether the model assumptions fit these skewed data.
lessons.r:
# Fictional clinic waits; no patient data.
wait <- c(12,15,14,18,21,16,19,13,45,17,20,22)
print(data.frame(Waiting_minutes=wait))
print(c(mean=mean(wait), median=median(wait), SD=sd(wait), SE=sd(wait)/sqrt(length(wait))))
# An illustrative Student t mean CI with 11 df, as in StatsDirect: only 12 skewed observations.
# Exact t coverage assumes independent normal observations; that is questionable here.
# A non-significant normality test would not establish the assumption.
mean_ci <- t.test(wait, conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("Illustrative 95% t interval for the mean; check assumptions:\n")
print(mean_ci)
# Describe this as about 13.8 to 24.8 minutes; keep full values for calculations.
# Extra displayed decimals do not make the assumptions more credible.
hist(wait, breaks=8, main="Fictional clinic waiting times", xlab="Minutes")
# Try: explain why mean and median differ; inspect the outlier without silently deleting it.
previousChallenges: Why would collecting four times as many independent observations halve the standard error but not necessarily change the standard deviation?

learningObjectives: Choose summaries that answer the substantive question.
Distinguish variability of observations from precision of estimates.
Interpret confidence intervals conditional on assumptions.

keyConcepts.explanation: SD describes variability between observations. SE describes variability of an estimator over repeated samples; they answer different questions.
A 95% procedure aims to cover the fixed population parameter in 95% of repetitions under its assumptions. It is not an interval containing 95% of individual observations.
Skew, unusual observations, clustering and selection affect interpretation. Increasing sample size alone does not correct biased recruitment or recording.

misconceptions.claim: The confidence interval describes where most individual waits lie.
misconceptions.correction: It describes uncertainty about a parameter; use the distribution or a suitable prediction interval for individuals.

misconceptions.claim: Delete the longest wait to make the data normal.
misconceptions.correction: First check its provenance; a genuine long wait is relevant to service experience.

workedExample.design: Twelve fictional independent clinic waits, including a long wait of 45 minutes.
workedExample.interpretation: The mean is about 19.3 minutes and the median 17.5. The illustrative 95% Student t interval for the population mean is about 13.8 to 24.8 minutes in both StatsDirect and R (11 degrees of freedom). With only 12 skewed observations, its coverage assumptions need scrutiny. One decimal place is enough for this explanation; extra software digits do not imply reliable precision, and a narrow interval would not rule out selection bias.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Which would you report for a typical wait, and which for total workload?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: The median can describe a typical wait; the mean relates to the total. Report context and distribution rather than declaring one always superior.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Why does quadrupling independent sample size halve the theoretical SE but not guarantee a narrower realised interval?
teachingPrompts.expectedReasoning: SE scales with 1/sqrt(n) at fixed population variance; estimated SD and critical values vary between samples.

lessons.title: Interpreting a diagnostic test
lessons.objective: Choose the right denominator for sensitivity, specificity and predictive value.
lessons.summary: Sensitivity is the proportion positive among people with the condition; specificity is the proportion negative among those without it. Predictive values condition on the test result instead. The fictional sample represents a population with 10% prevalence and a reliable reference diagnosis. Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity also need to be applicable to the intended case mix, threshold and reference standard.
lessons.challenge: If the condition becomes rarer while sensitivity and specificity stay the same, what happens to the proportion of positive results that are false positives?
lessons.steps: In the diagnostic grid, columns represent disease present/absent and rows test positive/negative: enter top row 72, 81 and bottom row 18, 729. These are true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives respectively. These fictional independent observations give sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%, PPV about 47.1% and NPV about 97.6%. For sensitivity, StatsDirect and R binom.test() both use the Clopper–Pearson exact binomial method: the 95% interval is about 70.2% to 87.7%. This interval concerns sensitivity, not PPV; matching inputs, confidence level and method should give matching limits apart from rounding.
lessons.r:
# Fictional diagnostic study. Rows: test result; columns: disease status.
tp <- 72; fn <- 18; fp <- 81; tn <- 729
counts <- matrix(c(tp,fp,fn,tn),nrow=2,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=list(Test=c("Positive","Negative"),Disease=c("Present","Absent")))
print(counts)
print(c(sensitivity=tp/(tp+fn), specificity=tn/(tn+fp), PPV=tp/(tp+fp), NPV=tn/(tn+fn)))
# Treat diagnoses as reliable and observations as independent.
# StatsDirect and binom.test use the same Clopper-Pearson exact binomial method.
# This is a sensitivity interval, not an interval for all four measures.
sensitivity_ci <- binom.test(tp,tp+fn,conf.level=0.95)$conf.int
cat("95% Clopper-Pearson exact CI for sensitivity (may be conservative):\n")
print(sensitivity_ci)
barplot(counts, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE, main="Fictional diagnostic counts", ylab="People")

learningObjectives: Use the correct conditional denominator for each accuracy measure.

keyConcepts.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity condition on reference disease status. Predictive values condition on the observed test result.
Prevalence changes predictive values when sensitivity and specificity are held fixed. Case mix, threshold and verification procedures may also change apparent accuracy.
LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity). Multiply pre-test odds by LR+, then convert post-test odds to probability. Multiplying probability by LR+ is incorrect.

misconceptions.claim: An 80% sensitive test means a positive result has an 80% probability of disease.
misconceptions.correction: That confuses sensitivity with positive predictive value.

misconceptions.claim: Accuracy measured in severe cases and healthy controls transfers unchanged to screening.
misconceptions.correction: The intended population may have a different spectrum of disease and alternative diagnoses.

workedExample.design: Fictional representative sample with a reliable reference diagnosis, 90 cases and 810 non-cases; a fixed test threshold.
workedExample.interpretation: 72 true positives and 81 false positives give PPV 72/153, about 47.1%, despite 80% sensitivity and 90% specificity. A positive result is not a certain diagnosis. Sensitivity is 80%, with the same 95% Clopper–Pearson interval of about 70.2% to 87.7% in StatsDirect and this R example.

lessons.title: Absolute and relative benefit
lessons.objective: Interpret absolute risk reduction, relative risk and the follow-up period.
lessons.summary: Over one year, 28/200 controls and 16/200 programme participants have at least one unplanned admission. The estimated absolute risk reduction (control minus programme) is 6 percentage points; programme-to-control RR is about 0.57 and NNT for benefit rounds up to 17. These are uncertain point estimates. The illustrated risk-difference interval includes zero and possible harm, so it does not establish benefit. This example was chosen to lie near the conventional 5% significance boundary: interpret the effect size and uncertainty, and do not choose a method just to obtain significance.
lessons.challenge: Would the same relative risk imply the same absolute benefit in a population with a much lower baseline risk?
lessons.steps: Assume individual randomisation, independent participants and complete one-year follow-up. In the NNT form enter 16 people with at least one admission among 200 programme participants and 28 among 200 controls. Count people, not repeated admissions. Interpret NNT 17 as the point estimate for preventing one additional person having an admission over one year. A risk-difference interval spanning zero gives NNT uncertainty extending through infinity into both benefit and harm; do not present a single ordinary finite NNT interval. The R script explicitly computes the same Miettinen–Nurminen score interval as StatsDirect, including its finite-sample variance correction; it does not use the simpler Wald interval from two-sample prop.test().
lessons.r:
# Fictional individually randomised programme; complete one-year follow-up.
# Events count people with at least one admission, not repeated admissions.
events <- c(16,28); totals <- c(200,200)
risk <- events/totals
print(data.frame(Group=c("Programme","Usual care"),Events=events,Total=totals,Risk=risk))
arr <- risk[2]-risk[1]
print(c(absolute_reduction=arr,relative_risk=risk[1]/risk[2],NNT=if(arr==0) Inf else ceiling(1/abs(arr))))
cat("NNT point-estimate direction:",if(arr>0) "benefit" else if(arr<0) "harm" else "no difference", "\n")

# Explicit Miettinen-Nurminen score interval, as used by StatsDirect.
# This base-R helper inverts the constrained-binomial score with the N/(N-1)
# variance correction. It also handles zero-event and all-event groups.
# Its direction is the first risk minus the second. No extra R package is needed.
mn_interval <- function(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level=0.95) {
  args <- c(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level)
  stopifnot(all(lengths(list(x1,n1,x0,n0,conf.level))==1), all(is.finite(args)),
            n1>=1,n0>=1,x1>=0,x1<=n1,x0>=0,x0<=n0,
            all(args[1:4]==floor(args[1:4])), conf.level>0,conf.level<1)
  estimate <- x1/n1-x0/n0
  critical <- qchisq(conf.level,df=1)
  score <- function(d) {
    lo <- max(0,-d); hi <- min(1,1-d)
    derivative <- function(p0) {
      term <- function(x,n,p) {
        (if(x==0) 0 else x/p) - (if(x==n) 0 else (n-x)/(1-p))
      }
      term(x1,n1,p0+d)+term(x0,n0,p0)
    }
    if(lo==hi) p0 <- lo else {
      rises <- (lo+d<=0 && x1>0) || (lo<=0 && x0>0) || derivative(lo)>0
      falls <- (hi+d>=1 && x1<n1) || (hi>=1 && x0<n0) || derivative(hi)<0
      p0 <- if(!rises) lo else if(!falls) hi else
        uniroot(derivative,c(lo,hi),tol=1e-14,check.conv=TRUE)$root
    }
    p1 <- min(1,max(0,p0+d))
    variance <- (p1*(1-p1)/n1+p0*(1-p0)/n0)*(n1+n0)/(n1+n0-1)
    if(variance<=0) return(if(estimate==d) -critical else Inf)
    (estimate-d)^2/variance-critical
  }
  limits <- c(lower=if(estimate<= -1) -1 else uniroot(score,c(-1,estimate),tol=1e-13,check.conv=TRUE)$root,
              upper=if(estimate>= 1) 1 else uniroot(score,c(estimate,1),tol=1e-13,check.conv=TRUE)$root)
  attr(limits,"conf.level") <- conf.level
  limits
}
# Keep the interval direction consistent with arr: usual care minus programme.
arr_ci <- mn_interval(events[2],totals[2],events[1],totals[1])
cat("95% Miettinen-Nurminen interval for risk reduction, usual care minus programme:\n")
print(arr_ci,digits=10)
# For the supplied counts this agrees with StatsDirect: about -0.001445 to 0.123548.
# Recalculate when changing the counts; these reference limits are not new data.
# This deliberately borderline example includes zero and possible harm.
# Do not change the method to seek a smaller P value. No single method is best
# for every design: these are independent binary outcomes, not paired/clustered data.
# Inverting an interval across zero needs separate benefit/harm branches via infinity.
# Do not report its reciprocals as one ordinary finite NNT interval.
barplot(risk,names.arg=c("Programme","Usual care"),ylim=c(0,0.2),ylab="One-year event risk")

learningObjectives: Report absolute and relative effects with the same outcome and time horizon.
Keep subtraction direction consistent across estimates and intervals.

keyConcepts.explanation: For this adverse outcome, control risk minus programme risk is the absolute risk reduction. Six percentage points is a difference of 0.06, not a 6% relative reduction.
An identical relative risk can imply different absolute differences in populations with different baseline risks, provided the relative effect is applicable.
NNT is a reciprocal of an absolute risk difference at a stated time horizon. If the difference interval crosses zero, its reciprocal has separate benefit and harm branches through infinity.

misconceptions.claim: An NNT point estimate of 17 establishes benefit.
misconceptions.correction: The interval for the underlying risk difference includes no effect and possible harm.

misconceptions.claim: NNT counts admissions prevented, including repeated admissions in the same person.

lessons.title: Association is not causation
lessons.objective: Interpret a regression slope without confusing prediction with causation.
lessons.summary: Each row is a different fictional service, with appointment duration and a mean satisfaction score on a 0–100 scale. The line describes a service-level association; it does not establish an individual-level or causal effect. Conventional small-sample regression inference assumes a linear conditional mean, independent errors with constant variance and normal errors. Inspect residuals and study design; the predictor need not be normally distributed.

Do not extrapolate beyond 10–24 minutes without justification.

# Eight fictional services: each row is a separate service, not a patient.
# Satisfaction is the service mean on a 0-100 scale.
# For conventional small-sample inference assume linear mean, independent,
# constant-variance normal errors. Predictor normality is not required.
data <- data.frame(Satisfaction=c(58,61,60,67,65,73,71,78),Minutes=c(10,12,14,16,18,20,22,24))
print(data)
fit <- lm(Satisfaction ~ Minutes, data=data)
print(summary(fit))
cat("95% confidence intervals for regression coefficients (not predictions):\n")
print(confint(fit,level=0.95))
plot(data$Minutes,data$Satisfaction,pch=19,xlab="Appointment minutes",ylab="Satisfaction",main="Association in fictional service data")
abline(fit)
plot(fitted(fit),residuals(fit),pch=19,xlab="Fitted satisfaction",ylab="Residual",main="Check the model, not just the slope")
abline(h=0,lty=2)
# Explain a potential service-level confounder; do not infer individual causation.

lessons.title: Comparing population rates
lessons.objective: Explain a crude rate difference using age-specific rates and a common standard population.
lessons.summary: A rate divides events by time at risk. Different age structures can produce different crude rates even when age-specific rates are identical. Direct standardisation applies the same reference weights to each population. A standardised rate is a comparison measure; report its reference population, uncertainty and age-specific pattern.
lessons.challenge: Two areas have identical younger and older age-specific rates but different crude rates. How could this happen, and what would a fair age-standardised comparison require?
lessons.steps: The worksheet has two rows: younger, then older. For Area A select Events (40, 800), Person-years (20000, 80000), then Reference population (75000, 25000) in Direct standardization. Use default row labels and multiplier 100000. The crude rate is 840 per 100000 person-years; the directly standardised rate is 400. Area B has 160 and 200 events in 80000 and 20000 person-years: its crude rate is 360 but the same standardised rate is 400. R displays both areas. Compare point estimates with matching units; StatsDirect also supplies intervals.
lessons.r:
# Fictional independent event counts; rows are younger, older.
# Person-time is time actually at risk, not the number of people enrolled.
area_a <- data.frame(Events=c(40,800),Person_years=c(20000,80000))
area_b <- data.frame(Events=c(160,200),Person_years=c(80000,20000))
reference <- c(75000,25000); weights <- reference/sum(reference)
rate_a <- area_a$Events/area_a$Person_years
rate_b <- area_b$Events/area_b$Person_years
crude <- c(A=sum(area_a$Events)/sum(area_a$Person_years),B=sum(area_b$Events)/sum(area_b$Person_years))*100000
standardised <- c(A=sum(weights*rate_a),B=sum(weights*rate_b))*100000
print(data.frame(Age=c("Younger","Older"),A_per_100000=rate_a*100000,B_per_100000=rate_b*100000,Weight=weights))
print(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised))
barplot(rbind(Crude=crude,Standardised=standardised),beside=TRUE,legend.text=TRUE,ylab="Events per 100000 person-years",main="Fictional areas, common age-specific rates")
# Point-estimate illustration. Do not give this weighted rate the CI for a single crude count.
# Equal standardised rates do not prove equality or remove all sources of bias.

lessons.objective: Explain what a numerical trial result can and cannot establish.
lessons.summary: Read the research question, allocation, follow-up and outcome measurement before the P value. Risk of bias concerns a particular result; reporting completeness and a large sample do not guarantee validity. Missing outcomes can break the comparability intended by randomisation. Explain effect size, uncertainty and applicability separately.
lessons.challenge: A randomised trial reports outcomes for 80 of 100 programme participants and all 100 controls. Before accepting its claim of benefit, what would you ask about the 20 missing outcomes?
lessons.steps: Fictional one-year adverse outcomes are observed in 20/80 programme participants and 30/100 controls. Try in StatsDirect opens the risk comparison: columns programme/control, top row events 20, 30; bottom row observed non-events 60, 70. The observed-data RR is 5/6. This omits 20 programme participants. R shows how their unknown outcomes permit full-group programme risks from 20% to 40%, against 30% in controls. These bounds describe missing-outcome uncertainty, not a 95% confidence interval.
lessons.r:
# Fictional individually randomised trial, one-year binary adverse outcome.
randomised <- c(Programme=100,Control=100)
observed <- c(Programme=80,Control=100)
events <- c(Programme=20,Control=30)
missing <- randomised-observed
print(data.frame(Randomised=randomised,Observed=observed,Events=events,Missing=missing))
observed_rr <- (events[1]/observed[1])/(events[2]/observed[2]); print(observed_rr)
programme_bounds <- c(Lower=20/100,Upper=(20+20)/100)
control_risk <- 30/100
arr_bounds <- c(Lower=control_risk-programme_bounds[2],Upper=control_risk-programme_bounds[1])
print(programme_bounds); print(arr_bounds)
plot(c(1,1),programme_bounds,type="b",pch=19,xlim=c(0.5,1.5),ylim=c(0,0.5),xaxt="n",xlab="Programme: possible one-year risk",ylab="Risk",main="Missing-outcome bounds, not a confidence interval")
abline(h=control_risk,lty=2)
legend("topleft", "Control risk: 30%", lty=2, bty="n")
# Bounds assume all 20 unknown outcomes are either non-events or events.
# They do not include sampling uncertainty or assert that either extreme is plausible.

lessons.objective: Describe missingness and avoid treating a filled-in value as observed information.
lessons.summary: Document the amount, pattern and reasons for missingness before choosing an analysis. MCAR, MAR and MNAR describe assumptions about the missingness process. MAR allows dependence on observed information; it is not a synonym for a random-looking pattern. Replacing missing values with a mean does not restore information or valid uncertainty.
lessons.challenge: Six of eight people return a symptom score. How might the interpretation change if the two missing people felt much worse, rather than simply forgetting an appointment?
lessons.steps: Scores range from 0 to 40, with higher scores worse. The StatsDirect worksheet contains only the six observed scores: 20, 22, 18, 26, 24, 30. Its mean is 23.33 for responders, not necessarily all eight people. R retains two explicit NA positions and shows full-group mean bounds of 17.5 to 27.5 if each missing score can lie anywhere from 0 to 40. This is an illustration of assumptions, not a confidence interval or a recommended imputation method.
lessons.r:
# Fictional scores, allowable range 0–40; higher is worse.
score <- c(20,22,18,26,24,30,NA,NA)
print(data.frame(Person=seq_along(score),Score=score,Missing=is.na(score)))
observed_mean <- mean(score,na.rm=TRUE)
mean_bounds <- (sum(score,na.rm=TRUE)+sum(is.na(score))*c(0,40))/length(score)
print(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Missing=sum(is.na(score))))
print(mean_bounds)
filled <- replace(score,is.na(score),observed_mean)
print(c(Observed_SD=sd(score,na.rm=TRUE),Mean_filled_SD=sd(filled)))
barplot(c(Observed_mean=observed_mean,Lower_bound=mean_bounds[1],Upper_bound=mean_bounds[2]),ylim=c(0,40),ylab="Symptom score",main="Missing values: bounds are not confidence limits")
# Mean filling is shown as a pitfall: it understates uncertainty if treated as real data.
# No method can identify the missing outcomes from these observed values alone.

lessons.summary: A model can rank outcomes well yet predict systematically wrong values. Evaluate calibration and prediction error as well as association. Performance on the development data is usually optimistic. Internal validation must repeat the modelling process; evaluation in a new relevant setting addresses transportability. A tiny illustration cannot establish clinical usefulness.
lessons.challenge: If we add ten points to every predicted score, can its correlation with observed scores stay unchanged while its prediction error gets worse?
lessons.steps: The fictional predictions were fixed before these eight outcomes were observed. Select Observed score as outcome and Predicted score as predictor in simple regression to inspect calibration; a descriptive calibration line is not a newly validated prediction model. R compares the original predictions with the same predictions shifted upward by ten. Correlation is unchanged; RMSE rises from about 1.58 to 10.12 points. Compare with the identity line, not just the fitted slope.

# Fictional independent evaluation sample. Predictions were fixed in advance.
predicted <- seq(10,80,by=10)
observed <- c(12,18,31,39,51,59,72,78)
shifted <- predicted+10
rmse <- function(p) sqrt(mean((observed-p)^2))
print(data.frame(Observed=observed,Predicted=predicted,Shifted=shifted))
metrics <- rbind(Original=c(Correlation=cor(observed,predicted),RMSE=rmse(predicted),Mean_error=mean(predicted-observed)),Shifted=c(Correlation=cor(observed,shifted),RMSE=rmse(shifted),Mean_error=mean(shifted-observed)))
print(metrics)
calibration <- lm(observed~predicted); print(coef(calibration))
plot(predicted,observed,pch=19,xlim=c(0,100),ylim=c(0,100),xlab="Predicted score",ylab="Observed score",main="Correlation does not establish calibration")
points(shifted,observed,pch=1,col="blue"); abline(0,1,lty=2)
legend("topleft",c("Original","Shifted +10","Ideal agreement"),pch=c(19,1,NA),lty=c(NA,NA,2),col=c("black","blue","black"))
# This eight-person example demonstrates metrics; it does not validate clinical use.
# Do not retune the model on these outcomes and then call the same data an untouched test set.

options.text: RMSE is unchanged because the ordering is unchanged.
options.feedback: RMSE depends on error size, not just ordering.

options.text: The new predictions are externally validated because correlation is high.
options.feedback: A metric alone cannot certify a validation design or usefulness.

options.text: Every observed outcome also increases by ten.
options.feedback: Only predictions were changed.

practiceQuestions.hint: Separate ranking from the numerical agreement between prediction and outcome.
practiceQuestions.lesson: A model can rank outcomes well yet predict systematically wrong values. Evaluate calibration and prediction error as well as association. Performance on the development data is usually optimistic. Internal validation must repeat the modelling process; evaluation in a new relevant setting addresses transportability. A tiny illustration cannot establish clinical usefulness.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Correlation is unchanged by an additive constant. With mean original error zero, shifting predictions by +10 gives mean error +10 and increases mean squared error by 100. Calibration and absolute prediction accuracy matter alongside association.

lessons.title: Combining study results
lessons.objective: Explain inverse-variance weighting and decide whether a pooled effect answers a coherent question.
lessons.summary: Pooling requires comparable populations, contrasts, outcomes and follow-up, together with an assessment of bias and dependence. Inverse-variance weights favour more precise estimates. A fixed-effect illustration assumes a common underlying effect. Random-effects models allow between-study variation but cannot repair biased studies or justify combining incompatible questions.
lessons.challenge: Three studies estimate the same risk difference, but one has twice the standard error of the others. Should it receive twice the weight, half the weight or a quarter of the weight?
lessons.steps: The fictional independent studies report one-year adverse-outcome risk differences (programme minus control) of −0.04, −0.08 and −0.03, with SEs 0.02, 0.04 and 0.02. In Summary meta-analysis choose Risk Difference, then Standard Error, and select the two named columns; use default study labels and 95% confidence. Compare the fixed-effect estimate with R: −4 percentage points, with a 95% normal interval of about −6.6 to −1.4 percentage points. Both use the inverse-variance common-effect estimate and a normal critical value. The R output retains unrounded values. This exercise assumes approximately normal estimates and a common underlying effect; it is not a complete systematic review.
lessons.r:
# Three fictional independent trials: same adverse outcome and one-year horizon.
# Risk difference = programme minus control. SE, not SD, is supplied.
effect <- c(-0.04,-0.08,-0.03); se <- c(0.02,0.04,0.02)
weight <- 1/se^2
pooled <- sum(weight*effect)/sum(weight)
pooled_se <- sqrt(1/sum(weight))
pooled_ci <- pooled+c(-1,1)*qnorm(0.975)*pooled_se
q <- sum(weight*(effect-pooled)^2)
print(data.frame(Study=1:3,Risk_difference=effect,SE=se,Percent_weight=100*weight/sum(weight)))
print(c(Pooled=pooled,SE=pooled_se,Lower=pooled_ci[1],Upper=pooled_ci[2],Q=q))
lower <- effect-qnorm(0.975)*se; upper <- effect+qnorm(0.975)*se
plot(effect,1:3,pch=19,xlim=range(c(lower,upper,0)),ylim=c(0,3.5),yaxt="n",xlab="Risk difference: programme minus control",ylab="",main="Fictional fixed-effect illustration")
segments(lower,1:3,upper,1:3); abline(v=0,lty=2)
points(pooled,0,pch=18); segments(pooled_ci[1],0,pooled_ci[2],0)
axis(2,at=0:3,labels=c("Pooled","Study 1","Study 2","Study 3"),las=1)
# The interval estimates a common effect under the model; not a prediction interval.
# Few studies give weak information about heterogeneity and publication bias.

# Optional further learning: conventional Q-based I-squared.
# Change FALSE to TRUE to run this extension after the main lesson.
if (FALSE) {
  study_df <- length(effect)-1
  i_squared <- if(q>0) 100*max(0,(q-study_df)/q) else 0
  print(c(Q=q,df=study_df,I_squared_percent=i_squared))
  # Here I-squared is 0%, after truncating a negative untruncated estimate.
  # Three studies give little information: 0% does not establish homogeneity.
  # Do not select fixed versus random effects just from Q's P value or I-squared.
}

learningObjectives: Calculate and interpret inverse-variance weights.
Keep effect directions, scales and time horizons consistent.
Distinguish a pooled-effect interval from between-setting variation.

keyConcepts.explanation: For independent approximately normal estimates with known or adequately estimated SEs, fixed-effect weights are 1/SE². Doubling SE gives one quarter of the weight.

A pooled-effect interval does not show the spread of true effects across settings. Examine clinical differences and heterogeneity uncertainty; a non-significant heterogeneity test with few studies proves little. Optional extension: conventional Q-based I² estimates the percentage of variation in study estimates attributable to heterogeneity. Here Q = 1.25 and df = 2, so max(0, (Q − df)/Q) × 100 = 0%. This truncated estimate is very uncertain with three studies and is not evidence of identical underlying effects.
Overlapping participants, selective reporting and unpublished results can undermine a synthesis. Choose eligible comparisons before looking at their P values.

misconceptions.claim: Meta-analysis always removes the biases of its component studies.
misconceptions.correction: Pooling may increase precision around a biased answer.

misconceptions.claim: Pick fixed or random effects solely from the heterogeneity P value.
misconceptions.correction: Choose the model to match the question and assumptions; examine variation and the uncertainty in estimating it.

workedExample.design: Three fictional independent trial estimates of the same one-year adverse-outcome risk difference, on an untransformed difference scale.
workedExample.interpretation: Weights are in the ratio 4:1:4, yielding a pooled difference of −0.04. Its model-based interval excludes zero, but this does not establish the quality, applicability or completeness of the underlying evidence.

teachingPrompts.prompt: Can two estimates from overlapping participant groups be entered as independent studies?
